CHAPTER 3.1 · LEARNING AREA 3

CHAPTER 3.1 · LEARNING AREA 3 · AUGUST · SEPTEMBER

Antiderivatives

In Year 12 you found the derivative of every function. Now it goes backwards: which function has this derivative? That is how speed turns into position and a rate of inflow into an amount of water. You learn the basic integrals up to $\tfrac1x$, the rules for sums and multiples, and you prove why two antiderivatives differ only by a constant. The CAS integrates everything else, and you check it.

10 LESSONS3 UNITSPROOF1 LAB
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • find antiderivatives, check them by differentiating and write down the indefinite integral
  • the basic integrals of powers with rational exponents, of $\mathrm{e}^x$, $\tfrac1x$, $\sin x$ and $\cos x$
  • integrate combined functions with the constant multiple and sum rules
  • prove that two antiderivatives on an interval differ only by a constant
  • integrate any function with the CAS, interpret results and verify them by differentiating

$f(x) = x^4$: what is $f'(1)$?

$f'(x) = 4x^3$

Written as a power, $\sqrt{x}$ is $x^r$. What is $r$?

$\sqrt{x} = x^{\frac12}$

$\left(x^{-2}\right)' = k \cdot x^{-3}$. What is $\tfrac{k}{4}$?

$k = -2$, so $\tfrac{k}{4} = -\tfrac12$

What is the derivative of $\sin x$?

$(\sin x)' = \cos x$

UNIT 13 LESSONS

1Antiderivative and indefinite integral

Which function has the derivative $2x$? $x^2$, but also $x^2 + 1$ and $x^2 - 7$: when you differentiate, every constant drops out, and when you work backwards you do not know it. All solutions have the form $x^2 + C$. Their graphs are shifted up and down against each other, and at every point they have the same gradient.

A function $F$ with $F'(x) = f(x)$ is called an antiderivative of $f$. So integration is the reverse of differentiation. Once you have found one antiderivative, you know them all: two antiderivatives of the same function differ only by a constant. The set of all antiderivatives is called the indefinite integral.

You always check an antiderivative the same way: differentiate it. If you get $f$, it is correct.

KEY POINT · ANTIDERIVATIVE AND INDEFINITE INTEGRAL

$F$ is an antiderivative of $f$ if $F'(x) = f(x)$ for all $x$.

If $F$ is one, every function $F + C$ is an antiderivative too, and on an interval there are no others. $C$ is called the constant of integration.

Indefinite integral: $\displaystyle\int f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = F(x) + C$   Say: “the integral of $f(x)$ with respect to $x$”.

The notation goes back to Leibniz: the $\int$ is a long S for “summa”, the sum. You will see why in chapter 3.2.

Reading off gradients: where $f$ is positive, every antiderivative $F$ increases; where $f$ changes sign, $F$ has a turning point.

THEOREM AND PROOF · ALL ANTIDERIVATIVES

Theorem: If $F$ and $G$ are two antiderivatives of $f$ on an interval $I$, then there is a number $C$ with $G(x) = F(x) + C$ for all $x \in I$.

Proof: Let $D(x) = G(x) - F(x)$. Then $D'(x) = G'(x) - F'(x) = f(x) - f(x) = 0$ for all $x \in I$. A function whose derivative is zero everywhere on an interval is neither strictly increasing nor strictly decreasing there: by the monotonicity theorem it is constant. So $D(x) = C$ and $G(x) = F(x) + C$. $\square$

The condition “interval” is needed: on $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$, $\ln|x|$ and $\ln|x| + \begin{cases} 1 & x > 0 \\ 0 & x < 0 \end{cases}$ are both antiderivatives of $\tfrac1x$, but they do not differ by one constant.

INTERACTIVE · F AND ITS ANTIDERIVATIVES

At the top an antiderivative $F$ with a constant $C$ you can move and its tangent, at the bottom $f$. The gradient of $F$ at every point is the value of $f$ there, however large $C$ is.

EXAMPLE 1 · CHECKING BY DIFFERENTIATING

Is $F(x) = x^3 - 2x + 5$ an antiderivative of $f(x) = 3x^2 - 2$? And $G(x) = x^3 - x^2$?

$F'(x) = 3x^2 - 2 = f(x)$ ✔ The 5 drops out when you differentiate.

$G'(x) = 3x^2 - 2x \neq f(x)$: $F$ yes, $G$ no.

EXAMPLE 2 · THROUGH A POINT

Find the antiderivative of $f(x) = 2x + 3$ whose graph passes through $P(1, 6)$.

All antiderivatives: $F(x) = x^2 + 3x + C$. Point test: $F(1) = 1 + 3 + C = 6$, so $C = 2$.

$F(x) = x^2 + 3x + 2$

EXERCISES

Check by differentiating whether $F$ is an antiderivative of $f$: a) $F(x) = x^4 + 1$, $f(x) = 4x^3$   b) $F(x) = -\cos x$, $f(x) = \sin x$   c) $F(x) = x^2 - 3$, $f(x) = x^2$

a) yes   b) yes, $(-\cos x)' = \sin x$   c) no, $F'(x) = 2x$

Give three different antiderivatives of $f(x) = 2x$ and sketch their graphs in one coordinate system.

For example $x^2$, $x^2 + 1$, $x^2 - 5$: three standard parabolas, shifted vertically against each other.

Find the antiderivative of $f(x) = 6x^2 - 4$ whose graph passes through $P(1, 3)$.

$F(x) = 2x^3 - 4x + C$, $F(1) = -2 + C = 3$: $F(x) = 2x^3 - 4x + 5$

$F$ is an antiderivative of $f(x) = x^2 - 4$. Where does $F$ have turning points? Of which kind?

$F' = f$: the turning points of $F$ are at the zeros of $f$ with a change of sign.

$f(x) = 0$ at $x = \pm 2$. At −2, $f$ changes from $+$ to $-$: maximum of $F$. At 2 from $-$ to $+$: minimum.

Explain without calculating, but with the theorem above: if $F$ and $G$ are antiderivatives of the same function and $F(2) = G(2)$, then $F = G$. Does this also hold if $F$ and $G$ are only defined on $(-\infty, 0) \cup (0, \infty)$?

What does the theorem say about $G - F$? For the second part, think of $\tfrac1x$.

On an interval, $G = F + C$. From $F(2) = G(2)$ it follows that $C = 0$, so $G = F$.

Not on two separate intervals: the constant may be different to the left and to the right of 0. Equality at $x = 2$ only fixes the constant on the right.

A lift travels upwards from a height of 10 m with the speed $v(t) = 4t$ (in m/s) as long as $t \le 2$. Find its height $s(t)$. How high is it after 2 seconds?

The height is an antiderivative of the speed: $s'(t) = v(t)$.

$s(t) = 2t^2 + C$ with $s(0) = 10$: $s(t) = 2t^2 + 10$. After 2 s: 18 m.

TEST YOURSELF!

The antiderivative $F$ of $f(x) = 2x$ passes through $(1, 5)$. What is $F(2)$?

$F(x) = x^2 + 4$

$\int x^3\,\mathrm{d}x = k \cdot x^4 + C$. What is $k$?

$\tfrac14$

Two antiderivatives of the same function on an interval …

$F$ and $F + C$

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Basic integrals and rules of integration

When you differentiate $x^n$, the exponent goes down by 1 and moves to the front as a factor. Backwards that means: raise the exponent by 1 and divide by the new exponent. Check for $x^4$: $\left(\tfrac{x^5}{5}\right)' = \tfrac{5x^4}{5} = x^4$ ✔

The rule holds for every exponent except −1, so also for roots and fractions if you first write them as powers: $\sqrt{x} = x^{\frac12}$, $\tfrac{1}{x^2} = x^{-2}$. For $r = -1$ there would be a zero in the denominator. The logarithm fills this gap: $(\ln x)' = \tfrac1x$.

As with differentiating, you may integrate term by term, and a constant factor simply stays.

KEY POINT · BASIC INTEGRALS AND RULES

Power rule: $\displaystyle\int x^r\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{x^{r+1}}{r+1} + C$ for every rational number $r \neq -1$

$\displaystyle\int \frac1x\,\mathrm{d}x = \ln|x| + C$ · $\displaystyle\int \mathrm{e}^x\,\mathrm{d}x = \mathrm{e}^x + C$ · $\displaystyle\int \sin x\,\mathrm{d}x = -\cos x + C$ · $\displaystyle\int \cos x\,\mathrm{d}x = \sin x + C$

Constant multiple rule: $\int k \cdot f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = k \cdot \int f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$ · Sum rule: $\int \big(f(x) + g(x)\big)\,\mathrm{d}x = \int f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x + \int g(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$

Why $|x|$? For $x < 0$, $\ln x$ is not defined, but $\left(\ln(-x)\right)' = \tfrac{-1}{-x} = \tfrac1x$. The modulus covers both sides.

Careful: there is no such simple rule for products. $\int x \cdot x\,\mathrm{d}x$ is not $\tfrac{x^2}{2} \cdot \tfrac{x^2}{2}$: multiply out first, $\int x^2\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac{x^3}{3} + C$.

INTERACTIVE · INTEGRATION TRAINER

Type in an antiderivative, for example x^4/4 - 3x, 2/3 x^(3/2) or -cos(x). The book checks whether it differs from a correct solution only by a constant; you may add a “+ C”.

EXAMPLE 3 · ROOTS AND FRACTIONS

Calculate $\displaystyle\int \left(4x^3 - 3\sqrt{x} + \frac{2}{x^2}\right)\mathrm{d}x$.

As powers: $4x^3 - 3x^{\frac12} + 2x^{-2}$. Term by term: $4 \cdot \tfrac{x^4}{4} - 3 \cdot \tfrac{x^{3/2}}{3/2} + 2 \cdot \tfrac{x^{-1}}{-1}$.

$x^4 - 2x^{\frac32} - \dfrac{2}{x} + C$. Check: $\left(-2x^{\frac32}\right)' = -3x^{\frac12}$ ✔, $\left(-2x^{-1}\right)' = 2x^{-2}$ ✔

EXAMPLE 4 · EXPONENTIAL FUNCTION, LOGARITHM, SINE

Calculate $\displaystyle\int \left(2\mathrm{e}^x - 3\sin x + \frac1x\right)\mathrm{d}x$.

$2\mathrm{e}^x - 3 \cdot (-\cos x) + \ln|x|$, so

$2\mathrm{e}^x + 3\cos x + \ln|x| + C$. Check: $(3\cos x)' = -3\sin x$ ✔

EXERCISES

Calculate: a) $\int (x^3 + 2x)\,\mathrm{d}x$   b) $\int 5\,\mathrm{d}x$   c) $\int (6x^2 - 4x + 1)\,\mathrm{d}x$

a) $\tfrac14 x^4 + x^2 + C$   b) $5x + C$   c) $2x^3 - 2x^2 + x + C$

Calculate: a) $\int \sqrt{x}\,\mathrm{d}x$   b) $\int \tfrac{1}{x^3}\,\mathrm{d}x$   c) $\int 3\cos x\,\mathrm{d}x$

a) $\tfrac23 x^{\frac32} + C$   b) $-\dfrac{1}{2x^2} + C$   c) $3\sin x + C$

Calculate $\displaystyle\int \frac{x^2 + 1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x$ for $x > 0$.

First split the fraction into two terms.

$\int \left(x + \tfrac1x\right)\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac12 x^2 + \ln x + C$

Calculate $\int (x + 2)^2\,\mathrm{d}x$ after multiplying out. Lea writes $\tfrac13 (x + 2)^3 + C$ instead. Is she right?

$\int (x^2 + 4x + 4)\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac13 x^3 + 2x^2 + 4x + C$. Lea's solution is correct too: $\tfrac13 (x + 2)^3 = \tfrac13 x^3 + 2x^2 + 4x + \tfrac83$, it differs only by the constant $\tfrac83$.

Prove the rule $\int \tfrac1x\,\mathrm{d}x = \ln|x| + C$ separately for $x > 0$ and for $x < 0$. Which rule of differentiation do you need in the second case?

$x > 0$: $|x| = x$, $(\ln x)' = \tfrac1x$ ✔

$x < 0$: $|x| = -x$, with the chain rule $\left(\ln(-x)\right)' = \tfrac{1}{-x} \cdot (-1) = \tfrac1x$ ✔ So on each of the two intervals $\ln|x|$ is an antiderivative.

Find the function $f$ with $f''(x) = 6x$, $f'(0) = -3$ and $f(0) = 2$. What do you notice about $f(1)$?

Integrate twice, and after each step find the constant from the condition.

$f'(x) = 3x^2 + C_1 = 3x^2 - 3$, $f(x) = x^3 - 3x + C_2 = x^3 - 3x + 2$. $f(1) = 0$ and $f'(1) = 0$: $x = 1$ is a double zero, $f(x) = (x - 1)^2 (x + 2)$.

TEST YOURSELF!

$\int \sqrt{x}\,\mathrm{d}x = k \cdot x^{\frac32} + C$. What is $k$?

Divide by $\tfrac32$: $\tfrac23$

$F$ is the antiderivative of $\tfrac1x$ with $F(1) = 0$. What is $F(\mathrm{e})$?

$F(x) = \ln x$, $\ln \mathrm{e} = 1$

$\int \sin x\,\mathrm{d}x = \ldots$

Check: $(-\cos x)' = \sin x$

UNIT 33 LESSONS

3Integrating with the CAS, verifying by hand

For $x\,\mathrm{e}^x$, $\sin(2x)$ or $\tfrac{2x}{x^2 + 1}$ the basic integrals are not enough. A CAS finds the antiderivatives at once, but it often shows a form you did not expect, and it leaves out the $+ C$. Whether a result is right is not decided by how it looks, but by its derivative.

You carry out a verification with the rules of differentiation from Year 12: the product rule for $u \cdot v$, the chain rule for compositions. If differentiating gives exactly the integrand, the antiderivative is proved. Two different results are both correct if their difference is constant.

Some functions have no antiderivative at all that can be written with the known functions, for example $\mathrm{e}^{-x^2}$, the bell curve from chapter 4. Then even the CAS can only calculate numerically, see chapter 3.4.

KEY POINT · CAS AND VERIFICATION

On the CAS: the command for the indefinite integral, enter the term and the variable, add the $+ C$ yourself.

Verification: $F$ is an antiderivative of $f$ $\iff$ $F'(x) = f(x)$. Two results $F_1$, $F_2$ belong to the same function if $F_1 - F_2$ is constant.

Useful for spotting: $\left(\ln g(x)\right)' = \dfrac{g'(x)}{g(x)}$ for $g(x) > 0$ and $\left(\mathrm{e}^{g(x)}\right)' = \mathrm{e}^{g(x)} \cdot g'(x)$.

On the CAS you can let it do the check as well: differentiate the result and subtract the integrand. If you get 0, it is correct.

Products such as $x\,\mathrm{e}^x$ are not integrated factor by factor: $\tfrac12 x^2 \cdot \mathrm{e}^x$ is wrong, the check shows it at once.

FIGURE · FUNCTION AND ANTIDERIVATIVE

$f(x) = 2x\,\mathrm{e}^{-x^2}$ and an antiderivative $F(x) = -\mathrm{e}^{-x^2}$ as the CAS gives it: where $f$ is positive, $F$ increases; at the zero of $f$, $F$ has its minimum.

EXAMPLE 5 · THE PRODUCT RULE AS A CHECK

A CAS gives $\int x\,\mathrm{e}^x\,\mathrm{d}x = (x - 1)\,\mathrm{e}^x$. Verify this.

$u = x - 1$, $v = \mathrm{e}^x$: $\left((x - 1)\,\mathrm{e}^x\right)' = 1 \cdot \mathrm{e}^x + (x - 1)\,\mathrm{e}^x = x\,\mathrm{e}^x$ ✔

$\int x\,\mathrm{e}^x\,\mathrm{d}x = (x - 1)\,\mathrm{e}^x + C$

EXAMPLE 6 · TWO CORRECT RESULTS

For $\int \sin(2x)\,\mathrm{d}x$ one CAS shows $\sin^2 x$, another $-\tfrac12 \cos(2x)$. Who is right?

Both derivatives are correct: $(\sin^2 x)' = 2\sin x \cos x = \sin(2x)$ and $\left(-\tfrac12 \cos(2x)\right)' = \sin(2x)$.

With $\cos(2x) = 1 - 2\sin^2 x$ we get $-\tfrac12 \cos(2x) = \sin^2 x - \tfrac12$: the results differ by the constant $\tfrac12$.

EXERCISES

Verify that $F$ is an antiderivative of $f$: a) $F(x) = \mathrm{e}^{x^2}$, $f(x) = 2x\,\mathrm{e}^{x^2}$   b) $F(x) = \sin(x^2)$, $f(x) = 2x \cos(x^2)$

Chain rule: a) $\mathrm{e}^{x^2} \cdot 2x$ ✔   b) $\cos(x^2) \cdot 2x$ ✔

A CAS gives $\int x\,\mathrm{e}^{2x}\,\mathrm{d}x = \left(\tfrac x2 - \tfrac14\right)\mathrm{e}^{2x}$. Confirm this by differentiating.

Product and chain rules: $\tfrac12 \mathrm{e}^{2x} + \left(\tfrac x2 - \tfrac14\right) \cdot 2\mathrm{e}^{2x} = \tfrac12 \mathrm{e}^{2x} + x\,\mathrm{e}^{2x} - \tfrac12 \mathrm{e}^{2x} = x\,\mathrm{e}^{2x}$ ✔

For $\int \dfrac{2x}{x^2 + 1}\,\mathrm{d}x$ the CAS shows $\ln(x^2 + 1)$. Verify this and explain why no absolute value is needed here.

$\left(\ln(x^2 + 1)\right)' = \dfrac{1}{x^2 + 1} \cdot 2x$ ✔ The absolute value is rightly missing, because $x^2 + 1 > 0$ for all $x$.

For $\int (x - 1)^2\,\mathrm{d}x$ the CAS gives the result $\tfrac13 x^3 - x^2 + x$, Max has $\tfrac13 (x - 1)^3$. Show that both are correct and find the constant by which they differ.

$\tfrac13 (x - 1)^3 = \tfrac13 x^3 - x^2 + x - \tfrac13$: both have the derivative $(x - 1)^2$, the difference is $\tfrac13$.

Lena claims: $\int \mathrm{e}^{x^2}\,\mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{\mathrm{e}^{x^2}}{2x} + C$, “because you have to divide by the inner derivative”. Disprove her by differentiating and explain why her recipe only works for a linear inner function.

Differentiate with the quotient rule, or $\tfrac{1}{2x} \cdot \mathrm{e}^{x^2}$ with the product rule.

$\left(\tfrac{1}{2x}\,\mathrm{e}^{x^2}\right)' = -\tfrac{1}{2x^2}\,\mathrm{e}^{x^2} + \tfrac{1}{2x} \cdot 2x\,\mathrm{e}^{x^2} = \mathrm{e}^{x^2} - \tfrac{\mathrm{e}^{x^2}}{2x^2} \neq \mathrm{e}^{x^2}$.

For $g(x) = ax + b$ the inner derivative is the constant $a$, and a constant factor passes through differentiation unchanged. For $x^2$ the inner derivative $2x$ depends on $x$ and is itself differentiated as well.

TEST YOURSELF!

By which constant do $\sin^2 x$ and $-\tfrac12 \cos(2x)$ differ?

$\cos(2x) = 1 - 2\sin^2 x$

$F(x) = \mathrm{e}^{x^2}$ is an antiderivative of $2x\,\mathrm{e}^{x^2}$. What is $F(1) - F(0)$ to three decimal places?

$\mathrm{e} - 1 \approx 1.718$

A CAS shows $\int x\,\mathrm{e}^x\,\mathrm{d}x = (x - 1)\,\mathrm{e}^x$. What is the quickest way to verify this?

Differentiating with the product rule gives $x\,\mathrm{e}^x$.

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

Calculate $\displaystyle\int \left(3x^2 - \frac2x + \mathrm{e}^x\right)\mathrm{d}x$ for $x > 0$.

$x^3 - 2\ln x + \mathrm{e}^x + C$

Connecting with Year 12: $F$ is an antiderivative of $f(x) = x^2 - 2x - 3$. Find the turning points and the points of inflection of $F$ without setting up $F$.

$f(x) = (x - 3)(x + 1)$. At $x = -1$, $f$ changes from $+$ to $-$: maximum of $F$; at $x = 3$ a minimum. Point of inflection of $F$: turning point of $f$, $f'(x) = 2x - 2 = 0$, so $x = 1$.

Which of the functions $F_1(x) = \sin^2 x$, $F_2(x) = -\cos^2 x$, $F_3(x) = \tfrac12 \sin^2 x$ are antiderivatives of $f(x) = \sin(2x)$? Give reasons.

$F_1' = 2\sin x \cos x = \sin(2x)$ ✔, $F_2' = 2\cos x \sin x = \sin(2x)$ ✔, $F_3' = \sin x \cos x = \tfrac12 \sin(2x)$ ✘. $F_1$ and $F_2$ differ by 1, because $\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1$.

Open problem: We are looking for a polynomial function $F$ of degree three whose derivative $f$ has zeros at $x = -1$ and $x = 2$ and whose graph passes through the origin. How many such $F$ are there? Give two different ones and describe how they are related.

$f(x) = a\,(x + 1)(x - 2)$ with $a \neq 0$, then integrate and substitute $F(0) = 0$.

$f(x) = a\,(x^2 - x - 2)$, $F(x) = a\left(\tfrac13 x^3 - \tfrac12 x^2 - 2x\right)$, the constant is 0 because $F(0) = 0$.

There are infinitely many, one for every $a \neq 0$, for example $a = 6$: $2x^3 - 3x^2 - 12x$ and $a = -6$: $-2x^3 + 3x^2 + 12x$. They arise from each other by stretching in the $y$-direction; the extreme points at −1 and 2 stay.

A train starts from rest with the constant acceleration $a(t) = 0.5$ m/s². Find $v(t)$ and $s(t)$ with $v(0) = 0$ and $s(0) = 0$. When has it travelled 1 km, and how fast is it then?

$v(t) = 0.5t$, $s(t) = 0.25t^2$. $0.25t^2 = 1000$: $t \approx 63.2$ s, then $v \approx 31.6$ m/s, about 114 km/h.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

Newton, Leibniz and the dispute over who was first

Differential and integral calculus were invented by two men independently of each other. Isaac Newton in England called his method “fluxions”. He wrote it down in 1671, but it was not printed until 1736, long after his death. Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, born in Leipzig in 1646, first wrote $\int f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$ in a note on 21 November 1675. In 1684 he published the differential calculus in the Leipzig journal Acta Eruditorum, and in 1686 his integral sign appeared there too.

Later, Newton's followers accused Leibniz of plagiarism. The Royal Society in London set up a committee whose report, early in 1713, found in Newton's favour. It had been written, without his name, by Newton himself: he had been President of the Society since 1703. Today both are regarded as inventors. But it was Leibniz's notation that won: the $\int$ and the $\mathrm{d}x$ you use in this chapter.

Source: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews: biographies “Gottfried Wilhelm von Leibniz” and “Isaac Newton”.

Proof: $(G - F)' = 0$, so $G - F$ is constant.

$\left((x - 1)\,\mathrm{e}^x\right)' = x\,\mathrm{e}^x$
